sections.text: अश्रद्धया हुतं दत्तं तपस्तप्तं कृतं च यत्।

Whatsoever is done without faith, whether it be sacrifice, austerity or gift or anything else, is called Asat (meaning Unreal) for it is the negation of Sat, O Arjuna! Such an act has no significance, here or hereafter.

We had been discussing chapter 17, Sraddhatriya Vipaga Yoga, and what we have seen so far in this chapter and in the Bhagavad Gita is that we have heard that our body is what we eat, our mind is what we think, and what we think is dependent on our faith, dependent on what we are convinced of or convicted of. So thinking is driven by our convictions. And therefore who I am is all about my convictions. So who I am is depending on my faith. And therefore this chapter elaborates what are the types of faiths a person can have? Then we have broadly classified, just as everything else, in three categories.
Faith can be Sattvic, faith can be Rajasic, faith can be Tamasic, and depending on that, I may be a Sattvic person, a Rajasic person or a Tamasik person, and my understanding of that will help me how do I change my faith so that my thinking changes, so my behavior changes, my mind changes and ultimately gives me the result which Im looking for, which is in the end is to achieve happiness. Youre all looking for one and one thing alone is to get out of our limitations and sorrows. So Bhagavan has described in this chapter the three types of faith and how it controls our Ahara, our Yagna, our Tapa and our Dana. As we have seen last time, it is what we take from this world, how we interact and connect with this world, how we discipline ourselves for what we want and then what we give back to this world, all dependent on my faith. And therefore my goal obviously is to make my faith more Sattvic. If I detect that I have Tamasic faith, I want to make it more Rajasic.
If I detect Im more Rajasya, make it Sattvik. Eventually I can get to my goal of achieving that happiness. So now our question was: well, I may or may not have that capability, and I may be all filled with Rajasic faith and not be able to change that. The last three verses we have seen say there is one way of mitigating that. There is a threefold indicator of that transcendental reality, the ultimate reality, the one unifying entity which binds us all, which is indicated in the Sastras as Om Tat Sat. Om is the transcendental form of the Lord that I have learned in the previous chapter. The Astadha Prakrithi, Eightfold manifest Prakriti of the Lord.
So everything which I see and perceive and feel is basically nothing but his manifestation. But then I come to the conclusion, maybe if I put everything together thats Lord, or if I put all the parts together, will it make a machine? The question is how you put it together. So all this part putting together does not still make the identity of the Lord. That is something beyond that. Lower Prakriti and higher Prakriti.
I have all these parts and say if I put all this together, it will be the whole. No, it has to be in a particular manner. Then only that machine functions as its supposed to be functioning. All these parts, I have to put it together and perceive it in a way that it will reveal the Lords identity. And thats the transcendental part, is how to see this whole in a manner that I can see Him. I see this world in its parts, but I cant put it together as his identity.
Thats the Aum, a transcendental part. Om is the indicator of that. And if I can remember that -- that all that I see, perceive, and experience put together -- I will never be able to fully understand the Lord through parts alone. But Om points to that reality beyond the parts. My faith may be rajasic, it may be even tamasic, but remembering Om will transform it into sattvic faith. Thats basically a way out given to us by these last three verses.
Om Tat Sat iti nirdeshah brahmanah trividhah smritah. These are the three indicators of that supreme reality. I know all the parts right now, but I cant put together the machine. I cant put together its real identity. So Aum is the one indicator. Tat we have seen is another indicator.
That is that that which I constantly keep referring to the God, the Lord, that entity other than this which I can perceive, feel, touch and vouch for it, that it exists. That which I cannot vouch for, that it exists, does exist, but beyond my perception. So thats Tat and Sat, the existence or the truth. Truth is that which exists in all periods of time. In other words, it was true yesterday, it is true today and it will be true tomorrow. That is Sat.
So these are the three indicators. And Bhagavan said that those who are Brahmavadina -- those who are completely convinced about the existence of that ultimate reality. Just like Mudivad (capitalism), Samajvad (socialism) -- because theyre convinced that this is the only way to help the society. Vaad means Im completely on the side of that.
Those who are completely convinced that Brahman is the only reality -- they will start all their activities by uttering Om. Utterance means remembrance. Its an indication to me that Om is the ultimate reality. I may be perceiving a difference between you and me right now, and therefore I may have developed a liking or disliking for you.
But Om is the ultimate reality which manifests as me, which manifests as you. As long as I have that thought in the beginning, whatever I do afterwards will be purified. Om Iti Udahritya Yajna Dana Tapaha Kriyaha -- we have discussed all that in the previous verses. The activities we are performing in this world:
We receive from the world, we interact with the world, we connect with this world, we prepare ourselves for how to interact with the world, and then we give back to the world. First, those who are Brahmavadina.
We see that those who are seeking liberation have come to the conclusion that there is no way that in my present state of limitedness the ultimate goal of infinite happiness is possible. I have come to that clear understanding that no matter how hard I try with my mind and intellect and body that unbroken happiness is not possible at all. Its only possible if I can identify with that. That which is unlimited. That which has no limitations.
That which has no sorrows, that which has no competition, that which is all-pervading. People who are seeking moksha -- and we are all Moksha Kankshi, believe it or not -- we want liberation from anything which we think is our limitation.
All of us who are aware of our limitations and are not happy with them -- if youre happy with your limitations, youre not a Moksha Kankshi. If I have some limitations but think this is good enough, then Im not seeking liberation. But we all have one limitation we cannot stand: running into a situation which makes me unhappy. Therefore Im constantly trying to avoid the things which create sorrows and want to pursue the things which give me happiness.
So at least I want to get rid of the limitations that run me into situations which give me unhappiness. Bhagavan says those Moksha Kankshi who want to get rid of those limitations will start all their activities -- the same yajna, tapa, dana kriyaha -- with Tat. Tat anabhisandhaya phalam yajna tapah kriyaha. They have come to the conclusion that if I remember Him as the Karma Phaladata, He is the giver of the fruits. So I leave the results to Him and do all my activities, trusting that He will give me the result that will lead to liberation.
We have learned that as Karma Yoga. The last one: sad bhave sadhu bhave cha sad iti etat prayujyate, prashaste karmani tatha sat shabdah partha yujyate. Sat is used in the sense of reality. Sat, as we have said is only that can be proven true in all three phases. In the past, in the present, in the future. Everything else is unreal. It existed one point of time in time and space, another period of time.
It has no existence whatsoever. Its completely gone. Just like a film on a screen or a hologram. It exists in my perception for a period of time. So the lamp is shut off. The word sat is used in the sense of reality and also for goodness.
Now we are coming back to the world which you and I know -- not transcendental unlimitedness, but the world of good and bad. Our world is divided by good and bad. Bhagavan said the real and the good is indicated in this world as Sat. As we say, there are values and there are universal values.
There are values may be applicable to me in this situation which may not be applicable in other situations. Well, those are transitory values. I work for a company and what are the values of the company? It only applies to me as long as I am there. But there are values which applies to me whether Im working or not. Whether Im working for this company or not or that company or not.
Those are universal values. Therefore we have said even before the civilization started, human beings knew what is right and what is wrong. Even before any religious were established, they knew what is good and what is bad. Those universal good and those universal truths are indicated as Sat. It is not dependent on any culture, not dependent on any beliefs -- those are the universal good and universal reality. So Bhagavan said, the word Sat is used in this sense of reality and of goodness. And also, Partha:
The word is used in the sense of auspiciousness. Anything which is good is auspicious. And therefore you start that work, same thing, yajna pohadana kriya with that word sat. Then may this be auspicious. May this act of mine be of goodness and of kindness and of reality. So you start with sat.
So obviously in the Sikh tradition, the word Sat is given the most importance: Sat Sri Akal, that Sat which is Akal, which is timeless, no beginning, no end. So that Sat is uttered: yajne tapasi dane cha sthitih sat iti uchyate. Therefore, if I am one who is clearly aware of good and bad in this world -- I divide my world into this is good and this is evil, this is good for me, this is bad for me -- then I should start all my activities with Sat. Bhagavan says yajne tapasi dane cha -- the activities remaining the same.
Whether it is my tamasic faith, my rajasic faith, or the sattvic faith, it is what my mind tells me is good, Im gonna do. No matter how much I tell you this is good for you, as long as your mind does not tell you it is good, you will not be able to follow. Everybody says, do this. Okay, okay, Ill think about it. But the thinking part never comes, because I have already decided it is not worth thinking about. So Bhagavan said -- and thats what yajne tapasi dane cha sthitih means:
To be steadfast in my yajna, dana, and tapa. I do some yajnas, but only occasionally -- some sacrifice here and there. But occasionally Im not steadfast. I sometimes get all excited and say, I think we should all do some charity or some kind of community service. We organize this, and then after about two weeks, everything gradually dies down.

This concluding verse delivers the chapters most sobering message: Asraddhaya hutam dattam tapas taptam krtam ca yat, asad ity ucyate partha na ca tat pretya no iha - whatever is offered, given, or practiced WITHOUT FAITH is called Asat (unreal, the negation of Sat), and has no significance here or hereafter. This is not about the object of faith, but about the presence of faith itself. Actions performed mechanically, rituals gone through without conviction, charity given without heart - all are rendered meaningless. Faith (shraddha) is the essential ingredient that transforms ordinary action into spiritual practice.
This verse invites deep self-examination: How much of your daily life is performed with genuine faith versus mere habit or obligation? Do you pray with conviction or recite words mechanically? Do you work with purpose or simply go through the motions? The teaching is both challenging and liberating - it is not the elaborate nature of your practice that matters, but the quality of faith behind it. A simple act done with complete faith surpasses grand gestures performed without heart. This week, choose one small daily action - perhaps your morning routine, a work task, or a family interaction - and infuse it with conscious intention and faith. Ask yourself before beginning: Do I truly believe in the value of what I am about to do? If not, either find that faith or reconsider the action. Remember: shraddha is the foundation upon which all spiritual transformation is built.
